lessons.title: Articles — El, La, Los, Las
lessons.explanation: Spanish nouns have gender (masculine/feminine). Definite articles: el (masc. singular), la (fem. singular), los (masc. plural), las (fem. plural). Indefinite articles: un, una, unos, unas.
examples: el libro (the book - masc.)
la casa (the house - fem.)
los niños (the children - masc. pl.)
las flores (the flowers - fem. pl.)
lessons.tip: Most nouns ending in -o are masculine (el libro); most ending in -a are feminine (la casa).

quiz.question: What article goes with 'casa' (house, feminine)?
What is the masculine plural definite article?

lessons.title: Subject Pronouns
lessons.explanation: Spanish pronouns: yo (I), tú (you-informal), él (he), ella (she), nosotros/nosotras (we), vosotros/vosotras (you-pl., Spain), ellos/ellas (they), usted (you-formal), ustedes (you-pl., Latin America).
examples: Yo soy estudiante. (I am a student.)
Tú hablas español. (You speak Spanish.)
Él es médico. (He is a doctor.)
Nosotros somos amigos. (We are friends.)
lessons.tip: In Spanish, subject pronouns are often omitted because the verb ending shows who is doing the action.

quiz.question: How do you say 'I' in Spanish?
Which pronoun means 'we' (masculine)?

lessons.title: Ser vs. Estar — Two Verbs for 'To Be'
lessons.explanation: Spanish has two verbs for 'to be'. SER: permanent qualities, identity, origin, profession. ESTAR: temporary states, location, feelings, conditions. This is one of the most important distinctions in Spanish!
examples: Yo soy español. (I am Spanish. - identity)
La ciudad está en España. (The city is in Spain. - location)
Él es médico. (He is a doctor. - profession)
Ella está cansada. (She is tired. - temporary state)
lessons.tip: Ser = permanent/essential. Estar = temporary/location. Ask: 'Is this a permanent characteristic?' to decide.

quiz.question: Which verb would you use for 'She is a teacher' (profession)?
Which verb for 'He is in the park' (location)?

lessons.title: Tener — To Have
lessons.explanation: The verb 'tener' (to have): tengo, tienes, tiene, tenemos, tenéis, tienen. Used for possession and many expressions.
examples: Tengo dos hermanos. (I have two brothers.)
¿Tienes hambre? (Are you hungry?)
Ella tiene 15 años. (She is 15 years old.)
Tenemos una reunión. (We have a meeting.)
lessons.tip: Tener is used for age in Spanish: ¿Cuántos años tienes? → Tengo doce años.

quiz.question: How do you say 'I have' in Spanish?
How do you say 'I am 10 years old' in Spanish?

lessons.title: Regular Verb Conjugation — Present Tense
lessons.explanation: Spanish verbs come in three groups: -AR, -ER, -IR. For -AR verbs (hablar): hablo, hablas, habla, hablamos, habláis, hablan. For -ER verbs (comer): como, comes, come, comemos, coméis, comen. For -IR verbs (vivir): vivo, vives, vive, vivimos, vivís, viven.
examples: Yo hablo español. (I speak Spanish.)
Tú comes pizza. (You eat pizza.)
Ella vive en Madrid. (She lives in Madrid.)
Nosotros trabajamos juntos. (We work together.)
lessons.tip: The key is to memorize one set of endings for each verb type. -AR verbs are the most common.

quiz.question: What is the 'yo' form of 'hablar'?
Which ending does 'él' take for -ER verbs?

lessons.title: Adjective Agreement
lessons.explanation: Spanish adjectives agree with the noun in gender and number. Most adjectives ending in -o: -o (masc. sg.) / -a (fem. sg.) / -os (masc. pl.) / -as (fem. pl.). Adjectives ending in -e or a consonant only change for plural.
examples: un chico alto (a tall boy)
una chica alta (a tall girl)
unos chicos altos (tall boys)
unas chicas altas (tall girls)
un estudiante inteligente / una estudiante inteligente
lessons.tip: In Spanish, adjectives usually come AFTER the noun: una casa grande (a big house).

quiz.question: How do you make 'bonito' (beautiful, masc.) feminine?

lessons.title: Possessive Adjectives
lessons.explanation: Spanish possessive adjectives (mi, tu, su, nuestro/a, vuestro/a, su) agree in number with the noun possessed; nuestro and vuestro also agree in gender. They usually come before the noun.
examples: mi libro (my book)
tus amigos (your friends)
nuestra casa (our house)
sus perros (his/her/their dogs)
lessons.tip: 'Su/sus' can mean his, her, its, your (formal), or their — context clarifies the meaning.

quiz.question: Which possessive agrees in both gender and number?
How do you say 'our house' (casa, feminine)?

lessons.title: Comparatives and Superlatives
lessons.explanation: Comparatives use más/menos...que (more/less...than) or tan...como (as...as). Superlatives use el/la/los/las + más/menos + adjective. Some adjectives have irregular forms: bueno→mejor, malo→peor.
examples: Ella es más alta que yo. (She is taller than me.)
Este libro es tan interesante como ese. (This book is as interesting as that one.)
Es el estudiante más inteligente de la clase. (He is the smartest student in the class.)
Mi hermano es menor que yo. (My brother is younger than me.)
lessons.tip: Watch for irregular comparatives: bueno→mejor (better), malo→peor (worse), grande→mayor (older/bigger), pequeño→menor (younger/smaller).

quiz.question: How do you say 'more...than' in a Spanish comparison?
What is the irregular comparative of 'bueno'?

lessons.title: Preterite — Past Tense
lessons.explanation: The preterite (pretérito indefinido) expresses completed past actions. -AR endings: -é, -aste, -ó, -amos, -asteis, -aron. -ER/-IR endings: -í, -iste, -ió, -imos, -isteis, -ieron. Many common verbs are irregular: ser/ir → fui, fuse, fue…
examples: Ayer comí pizza. (Yesterday I ate pizza.)
Él habló con el profesor. (He spoke with the teacher.)
Fuimos al cine. (We went to the cinema.)
¿Dónde viviste antes? (Where did you live before?)
lessons.tip: The preterite is for specific, completed events. Notice the accent marks — they distinguish yo form from él form.

quiz.question: What is the 'yo' preterite of 'hablar'?

lessons.title: Imperfect Tense (vs. Preterite)
lessons.explanation: The imperfect (pretérito imperfecto) describes ongoing, habitual, or background past actions, unlike the preterite which marks completed events. -AR endings: -aba, -abas, -aba, -ábamos, -abais, -aban. -ER/-IR endings: -ía, -ías, -ía, -íamos, -íais, -ían. Only ser, ir, and ver are irregular.
examples: Cuando era niño, jugaba mucho. (When I was a child, I used to play a lot.)
Ella vivía en Madrid. (She used to live in Madrid.)
Hacía sol cuando salimos. (It was sunny when we left.)
Íbamos a la playa todos los veranos. (We used to go to the beach every summer.)
lessons.tip: Use imperfect for descriptions, habits, and background; use preterite for specific completed events — they often appear together in the same story.

quiz.question: Which tense describes habitual past actions?
What is the 'yo' imperfect form of 'ser'?

lessons.title: Reflexive Verbs
lessons.explanation: Reflexive verbs describe actions the subject does to themselves, marked with reflexive pronouns (me, te, se, nos, os, se) placed before the conjugated verb. Common reflexive verbs: levantarse, ducharse, vestirse, lavarse.
examples: Me levanto a las siete. (I get up at seven.)
Ella se ducha por la mañana. (She showers in the morning.)
¿Te vistes rápido? (Do you get dressed quickly?)
Nos lavamos las manos. (We wash our hands.)
lessons.tip: With infinitives, the reflexive pronoun can attach to the end of the verb: voy a levantarme = me voy a levantar.

quiz.question: Which pronoun goes with 'nosotros' in reflexive verbs?
What does 'se ducha' mean?

lessons.title: Future Tense
lessons.explanation: The simple future (futuro simple) is formed by adding endings directly to the infinitive: -é, -ás, -á, -emos, -éis, -án — the same endings for all three verb groups. Some common verbs have irregular stems (tener→tendr-, hacer→har-, poder→podr-).
examples: Hablaré con ella mañana. (I will speak with her tomorrow.)
¿Vendrás a la fiesta? (Will you come to the party?)
Tendremos una reunión. (We will have a meeting.)
Ellos vivirán en Chile. (They will live in Chile.)
lessons.tip: Future endings attach directly to the full infinitive — no need to remove -ar/-er/-ir first.

quiz.question: What is the 'yo' future form of 'hablar'?
What is the irregular future stem of 'tener'?

lessons.title: El Subjuntivo — Subjunctive
lessons.explanation: The subjunctive expresses wishes, doubts, emotions, recommendations, and hypotheticals. Formed by taking the yo present form, dropping -o, and adding opposite vowel endings (-AR → -e endings; -ER/-IR → -a endings).
examples: Quiero que vengas. (I want you to come.)
Es importante que estudies. (It's important that you study.)
Ojalá que llueva. (I hope it rains.)
No creo que tenga razón. (I don't think he is right.)
lessons.tip: WEIRDO: Wish, Emotion, Impersonal expressions, Recommendation, Doubt/Denial, Ojalá — these trigger the subjunctive.

quiz.question: Which phrase triggers the subjunctive?

lessons.title: Conditional Tense and 'If' Clauses
lessons.explanation: The conditional (condicional) expresses hypothetical actions ('would'), formed with the same endings as the imperfect (-ía, -ías, -ía, -íamos, -íais, -ían) attached to the infinitive or an irregular stem. It pairs with the imperfect subjunctive in unreal 'si' clauses.
examples: Yo hablaría con ella. (I would speak with her.)
Si tuviera dinero, viajaría. (If I had money, I would travel.)
¿Podrías ayudarme? (Could you help me?)
Si fuera rico, compraría una casa. (If I were rich, I would buy a house.)
lessons.tip: The pattern 'si + imperfect subjunctive, + conditional' expresses hypothetical or contrary-to-fact situations.

quiz.question: What ending set does the conditional use?
In 'Si tuviera dinero, viajaría,' which mood is 'tuviera'?

lessons.title: Compound Tenses — Present Perfect and Pluperfect
lessons.explanation: Compound tenses use haber (conjugated) plus a past participle. The present perfect (he/has/ha/hemos/habéis/han + participle) describes past actions relevant to now; the pluperfect (había/habías... + participle) describes an action before another past action.
examples: He terminado mi tarea. (I have finished my homework.)
Ella ya había salido cuando llegué. (She had already left when I arrived.)
¿Habéis comido? (Have you all eaten?)
Nunca habíamos visto algo así. (We had never seen anything like that.)
lessons.tip: The participle never changes with haber — it stays in its -ado/-ido form regardless of the subject.

quiz.question: Which auxiliary verb forms Spanish compound tenses?
Which tense describes an action that happened before another past action?

lessons.title: Commands — Imperative Mood
lessons.explanation: Spanish commands differ by formality. Affirmative tú commands generally use the él/ella present indicative form (with irregulars: di, haz, ve, pon, sal, sé, ten, ven). Negative tú commands and all usted/ustedes commands use the subjunctive form.
examples: ¡Habla más despacio! (Speak more slowly! — tú affirmative)
¡No hables tan rápido! (Don't speak so fast! — tú negative)
Coma frutas, por favor. (Eat fruits, please. — usted)
¡Ven aquí! (Come here! — tú irregular)
lessons.tip: Negative commands always use the subjunctive form, even for tú — this differs from affirmative tú commands.

quiz.question: What form do affirmative tú commands usually use?
What mood do negative commands use?
